sense: one who judges books, plays, films or art

evidence: Cic. Or. 112: ut existimātōrēs videāmur loquī, nōn magistrī
terms.comment: Rare but classical: Cicero’s word for the knowing judge of oratory, as against the orator himself (magis existimātor metuendus quam admīrandus ōrātor, Brut. 146). Morgan–Owens gives it for a reviewer of books, films and plays, and existimātiō for a review.
Greek κριτικός: in Horace and Quintilian the scholars who judged the old poets. As an adjective Lewis & Short has it only in medicine (a critical stage of an illness).
The Alexandrian editor of Homer, whose name stood for a strict critic.

phrases.latin: ut existimātōrēs videāmur loquī, nōn magistrī
phrases.english: so that we may seem to speak as critics, not as teachers

phrases.latin: Ennius, et sapiēns et fortis et alter Homērus, ut criticī dīcunt
phrases.english: Ennius, wise and brave and a second Homer, as the critics say

phrases.latin: tōtum hunc locum, quem ego variē meīs ōrātiōnibus, quārum tū Aristarchus es, soleō pingere
phrases.english: this whole theme, which I like to paint in various colours in my speeches, whose Aristarchus you are

phrases.latin: arguet ambiguē dictum, mūtanda notābit: fīet Aristarchus
phrases.english: he will censure what is ambiguously put and mark what needs changing: he will turn Aristarchus
